title: Backtesting & Simulation
hook: Backtesting asks: would this strategy have worked? Simulation asks: could it work under conditions history never showed us?

keyterms.def: Applying an investment rule to historical data to estimate how a strategy would have performed out-of-sample in the past.
Using data in a backtest that was not actually available or knowable at the decision date, e.g. as-reported earnings before release.
Testing only on securities that still exist today, omitting delisted/failed names, which inflates returns and understates risk.
Over-mining the same data to find rules that fit past noise; also called overfitting or p-hacking, producing spurious signals.
Partitioning data into training and validation subsets to tune and test a model on data not used to build it.
Repeatedly re-estimating and re-forming the portfolio over a sliding fixed-length window that moves forward through time.
Generating many random return paths from an assumed distribution to estimate the full range of possible strategy outcomes.
Re-running simulations while changing input assumptions (mean, volatility, tails) to test how robust conclusions are.

body: Backtesting estimates how an investment strategy would have performed had it been implemented in the past. Its core objective is to build confidence that a rule captures a genuine, repeatable edge rather than luck, and to understand the strategy's risk before committing capital.

The standard process runs in stages: strategy design (define the investment universe, signal, rebalancing frequency, and constraints); historical investment simulation (form the portfolio period by period using only information available then); and performance analysis (compute returns, risk, and factor exposures).

A key design choice is rebalancing. A rolling-window approach re-estimates the model and reconstitutes the portfolio each period, mimicking how a manager would actually update decisions as new data arrives.

Judge a factor strategy on risk-adjusted terms, not raw return. The Sharpe ratio measures excess return per unit of total volatility; the information ratio measures active return per unit of tracking error versus a benchmark. Also inspect maximum drawdown (worst peak-to-trough loss) and downside deviation.

Return distributions matter: negative skew and high kurtosis warn that averages hide fat-tailed loss risk. A high mean with deep drawdowns and left-skew is more fragile than a modestly lower, symmetric one.

Common visuals: cumulative return curves (smoothness signals consistency), rolling Sharpe/IR plots (is the edge stable or decaying?), drawdown charts, and factor-return correlation heat maps to check whether apparent alpha is really disguised known-factor beta.
sections.formula:
Sharpe = (Rp - Rf) / sigma_p
IR = (Rp - Rb) / TrackingError

callout.label: RISK FIRST
callout.text: Two strategies with equal mean return can differ hugely in drawdown and skew; always rank on risk-adjusted and tail metrics.

body: Survivorship bias: building the test universe from securities that exist today drops firms that went bankrupt, delisted, or merged away. Because losers are removed, backtested returns look too high and risk too low. Fix: use a point-in-time database that includes dead securities.

Look-ahead bias: using information in a decision that was not yet available at that date. Examples: financial statements before their filing date, restated data, or benchmark constituents defined with hindsight. Fix: lag data to its true availability and use as-first-reported values.

Data snooping / overfitting: testing thousands of variations until one fits past noise. The winning rule then fails live. Fix: reserve untouched out-of-sample data, limit the number of trials, and demand economic rationale for the signal.

callout.label: LOOK-AHEAD vs SURVIVORSHIP
callout.text: Survivorship = WRONG sample (dead names dropped). Look-ahead = RIGHT sample but using data too early (not yet knowable at the decision date).

body: Because a single train/test split can be lucky, cross-validation repeatedly rotates which data trains the model and which validates it, then averages performance. This gives a more stable estimate of out-of-sample skill and helps detect overfitting.
With time-series data, ordinary random k-fold splitting can leak the future into the past. Use time-aware schemes instead: always train on earlier data and validate on strictly later data.

Two rolling schemes: a walk-forward (expanding) window keeps adding new data to a growing training set, while a fixed rolling window keeps the training length constant, dropping the oldest observations. Fixed windows adapt faster to regime change; expanding windows use more data and are more stable.
sections.formula: Walk-forward: train[t0..t], test[t+1]; then slide t forward

body: Historical simulation resamples or replays actual past returns, so it preserves the real, observed dependence, skew, and fat tails of markets. Its weakness: it is limited to scenarios that actually happened and can be dominated by one unusual episode.

Monte Carlo simulation draws returns from an assumed statistical distribution (often with specified means, volatilities, and correlations), generating thousands of hypothetical paths. It can explore outcomes history never produced and stress rare events, but its results are only as valid as the assumed distribution.

Use historical simulation when you trust that the past sample represents future dynamics; use Monte Carlo when you need a richer range of outcomes or want to inject specific tail or correlation assumptions.

callout.label: CORE DIFFERENCE
callout.text: Historical = replay real data (no distribution assumed). Monte Carlo = generate synthetic paths from an assumed distribution.

body: A Monte Carlo result is conditional on its inputs, so robust analysis varies those inputs. In sensitivity analysis you re-run the simulation while altering the assumed return distribution and observe how conclusions shift.

Typical changes: raise volatility, shift the mean lower, increase correlations toward 1 (diversification vanishes in crises), or swap a normal distribution for a fat-tailed one such as Student's t to capture extreme moves.

If the strategy's Sharpe, drawdown, or shortfall probability stay acceptable across these altered assumptions, conclusions are robust. If modest changes flip the verdict, the strategy is fragile and the base-case backtest overstated its reliability.
sections.formula: Multivariate draw: R = mu + L*z, where L*L' = Sigma (Cholesky)

flow: Design strategy: define universe, signal, constraints, rebalancing
Assemble point-in-time data; lag inputs to true availability
Analyze risk-adjusted metrics, drawdown, skew, factor exposures
Cross-validate out-of-sample; check for the three biases
Extend with Monte Carlo and sensitivity analysis on assumptions

quiz.q: A backtest builds its universe from stocks currently in the index and reports a very high Sharpe ratio. Which bias is most likely inflating results?
o: Survivorship bias
Look-ahead bias
Data snooping
quiz.e: Using only currently existing constituents drops delisted/failed firms, so losers are excluded and returns are overstated. That is survivorship bias.

quiz.q: An analyst ranks stocks on annual earnings using the fiscal-year-end date rather than the later filing date. Which bias does this create?
o: Survivorship bias
Look-ahead bias
Data snooping
quiz.e: The earnings were not public until the filing date; acting on them at fiscal year-end uses information not yet knowable, which is look-ahead bias. The sample itself is fine.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes look-ahead bias from survivorship bias?
o: Look-ahead uses data too early on the correct sample; survivorship uses a sample that wrongly excludes dead securities
They are identical; both drop failed firms
Look-ahead only affects Monte Carlo, survivorship only affects historical simulation
quiz.e: Survivorship is a sample-composition error (dead names removed). Look-ahead keeps the right sample but uses information before it was available at the decision date.

quiz.q: A team tests 5,000 signal variations and reports the single best one, which then fails live. This most directly illustrates:
o: Data snooping / overfitting
Survivorship bias
Rolling-window error
quiz.e: Mining many variants on the same data finds rules that fit past noise; the winner does not generalize. This is data snooping / overfitting.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly contrasts historical and Monte Carlo simulation?
o: Historical replays actual past returns; Monte Carlo generates paths from an assumed distribution
Historical assumes normality; Monte Carlo only uses realized data
Both require the same fixed number of scenarios
quiz.e: Historical simulation reuses observed data (no distribution assumed), while Monte Carlo draws synthetic paths from a specified distribution, allowing unseen scenarios.

quiz.q: Why should time-series backtests avoid ordinary random k-fold cross-validation?
o: It can train on future data and validate on the past, leaking information
It always overstates volatility
It cannot compute a Sharpe ratio
quiz.e: Random folds mix time order, letting future observations inform predictions of the past. Time-aware (walk-forward) splitting keeps training strictly before validation.

quiz.q: In sensitivity analysis, an analyst replaces the normal return assumption with a fat-tailed Student's t and raises correlations. What is the purpose?
o: To test whether conclusions remain robust under adverse assumptions
To eliminate survivorship bias
To reduce the number of Monte Carlo trials
quiz.e: Altering distribution and correlation inputs checks how sensitive the results are; robustness across stressed assumptions builds confidence, fragility warns of overstated backtests.

quiz.q: A factor backtest shows high average return but deep drawdowns and strong negative skew. The best interpretation is:
o: The strategy carries hidden tail risk despite the attractive mean
It is clearly superior because mean return is highest
Skewness is irrelevant to strategy selection
quiz.e: Negative skew and large drawdowns signal fat-tailed downside; the high mean masks fragility, so risk-adjusted and tail metrics must drive the judgment.
